title: I. The Breath Of Corruption
paragraphs: The body of Father Zossima was prepared for burial according to the established ritual. As is well known, the bodies of dead monks and hermits are not washed. The Church Ritual says: “If any one of the monks departs in the Lord, the monk designated (that is, the one whose office it is) shall wipe the body with warm water. First he shall make the sign of the cross with a sponge on the forehead of the deceased, on the breast, on the hands and feet and on the knees, and that is enough.” Father Païssy did all this himself. Then he dressed the deceased in his monastic garb and wrapped him in his cloak. By custom the cloak was slit a little, so that it could be folded around him in the form of a cross. On his head he put a hood with an eight-cornered cross. The hood was left open, and the dead man’s face was covered with black gauze. An icon of the Saviour was put in his hands. Toward morning he was laid in the coffin, which had been made ready long before. It was decided to leave the coffin in the cell all day, in the larger room where the elder used to receive his visitors and fellow monks. The deceased had been a priest and a monk of the strictest rule, so the Gospel, not the Psalter, had to be read over his body, by monks in holy orders. Father Iosif began the reading right after the requiem service. Father Païssy wanted to go on reading the Gospel over his dead friend all day and all night afterward. For the present, though, he and the Father Superintendent of the Hermitage were both very busy and occupied. Something extraordinary had begun to show among the monks, the visitors from the monastery hostels and the crowds flocking from the town: an unheard-of, even “unseemly” excitement and impatient expectation. As time went on, it became more and more marked. The Superintendent and Father Païssy did their utmost to calm the general bustle and agitation.

When it was fully daylight, some people began bringing their sick from the town, mostly children. It was as though they had been waiting for exactly this moment. They were plainly convinced that the dead elder’s remains had the power to heal, and that this would show itself at once, in keeping with their faith. Only then did it become clear how completely everyone in our town had accepted Father Zossima as a great saint while he lived. And those who came were far from all being of the humbler classes.

Father Païssy found this intense expectation among the believers unseemly, displayed as it was with such haste and openness, even with impatience and almost insistence. He had long foreseen something of the sort, but the actual show of feeling went beyond anything he had expected. Whenever he came across monks who showed this excitement, he began to reprove them. “Expecting something extraordinary so immediately,” he said, “shows a levity that is possible in worldly people but unseemly in us.”

But little attention was paid to him, and Father Païssy noticed it uneasily. Yet he himself (if the whole truth must be told) secretly cherished, at the bottom of his heart, almost the same hopes, and could not help knowing it. He was indignant at the too impatient expectation around him, and saw in it light-mindedness and vanity. Even so, it was particularly unpleasant to him to meet certain persons whose presence filled him with serious misgivings. In the crowd in the dead man’s cell he noticed, with an inward aversion (for which he at once reproached himself), Rakitin and the monk from Obdorsk, who was still staying in the monastery. Of both of them Father Païssy felt suddenly suspicious for some reason—though, indeed, he might well have felt the same about others.

Of everyone in that excited crowd, the monk from Obdorsk fussed the most. You met him wherever you turned. He asked questions here and listened there, and all around he whispered with a strange, secretive manner. Impatience was written all over his face, and even a kind of irritation.

As for Rakitin, as came out later, he had come to the hermitage so early at the special request of Madame Hohlakov. She was a good-hearted but weak-minded woman, and she could not have been admitted to the hermitage herself. As soon as she woke and heard of Father Zossima’s death, such intense curiosity seized her that she sent Rakitin off at once. He was to keep a careful lookout and report to her by letter every half-hour or so “_everything that takes place_.” She regarded Rakitin as a most religious and devout young man. He was particularly clever at getting around people and taking on whatever part he thought most to their taste, whenever he saw the slightest advantage in it for himself.

The day was bright and clear, and many of the visitors were crowding among the tombs. There were especially many of these around the church, and more were scattered about the hermitage. Walking around the grounds, Father Païssy thought of Alyosha. He had not seen him for some time, in fact not since the night. The moment he thought of him, he spotted him in the farthest corner of the hermitage garden. Alyosha was sitting on the tombstone of a monk who had been famous long ago for his saintliness. His back was to the hermitage and his face to the wall, and he seemed to be hiding behind the stone. Father Païssy went up and saw that he was weeping quietly but bitterly, with his face in his hands, and that sobs were shaking his whole body. Father Païssy stood over him for a little.

“Enough, dear son, enough, dear,” he said at last, with feeling. “Why are you weeping? Rejoice, do not weep. Don’t you know this is the greatest of his days? Just think where he is now, at this very moment!”
Alyosha glanced at him and uncovered his face, which was swollen with crying like a child’s. But he turned away at once without a word and hid his face in his hands again.
“Maybe it is well,” said Father Païssy thoughtfully. “Weep if you must. Christ has sent you those tears.”

“Your touching tears are only a relief to your spirit, and they will help to gladden your dear heart,” he added to himself as he walked away from Alyosha, thinking of him lovingly. He moved away quickly, though, because he felt that he too might weep, looking at him.

Meanwhile time was passing. The monastery services and the requiems for the dead followed in their due course. Father Païssy again took Father Iosif’s place by the coffin and began reading the Gospel. But before three o’clock in the afternoon, the thing took place that I alluded to at the end of the last book. It was so unexpected by all of us and so contrary to the general hope that, I repeat, this trivial incident is remembered in minute detail to this day in our town and all the surrounding neighborhood. I may add, for myself personally, that I find it almost repulsive to recall that event. It caused such frivolous agitation and was a stumbling block to so many, though in reality it was the most natural and trivial matter. I should of course have left it out of my story altogether, if it had not had a very strong influence on the heart and soul of the chief, though future, hero of my story, Alyosha. It formed a crisis and turning point in his spiritual development. It gave a shock to his intellect, which in the end strengthened it for the rest of his life and gave it a definite aim.

And so, to return to our story. Before dawn, when they laid Father Zossima’s body in the coffin and brought it into the front room, the people around the coffin raised the question of opening the windows. But this suggestion, made casually by someone, got no answer and was almost unnoticed. Some of those present may perhaps have noticed it inwardly, only to think that expecting decay and corruption from the body of such a saint was an actual absurdity. It called for pity (if not a smile) for the lack of faith and the frivolity it implied. For they expected something quite different.

And, behold, soon after midday there were signs of something. At first they were observed only in silence by those who came in and out, each evidently afraid to share the thought in his mind. But by three o’clock the signs had become so clear and unmistakable that the news quickly reached all the monks and visitors in the hermitage. It soon made its way to the monastery and threw all the monks into amazement. Finally, in the shortest possible time, it spread to the town and excited everyone in it, believers and unbelievers alike. The unbelievers rejoiced. As for the believers, some of them rejoiced even more than the unbelievers, for “men love the downfall and disgrace of the righteous,” as the deceased elder had said in one of his exhortations.

The fact is that a smell of decomposition began to come from the coffin. It grew gradually stronger, and by three o’clock it was quite unmistakable. In all the past history of our monastery no such scandal could be recalled. And in no other circumstances could such a scandal have been possible as the one that showed itself, in unseemly disorder, among the very monks themselves immediately after this discovery. Afterward, even many years afterward, some sensible monks were amazed and horrified when they recalled that day, that the scandal could have reached such proportions. For in the past, monks of very holy life had died, God-fearing old men whose saintliness was acknowledged by all. Yet from their humble coffins too the breath of corruption had come, naturally, as from all dead bodies, and that had caused no scandal or even the slightest excitement. Of course there had been saints in the monastery in former times whose memory was carefully preserved and whose relics, according to tradition, showed no signs of corruption. The monks regarded this fact as touching and mysterious. They cherished the tradition of it as something blessed and miraculous, and as a promise, by God’s grace, of still greater glory from those tombs in the future.

One of these, whose memory was especially cherished, was an old monk named Job, who had died seventy years before at the age of a hundred and five. He had been a celebrated ascetic, strict in fasting and silence. His tomb was pointed out to every visitor on arrival with peculiar respect and mysterious hints of great hopes connected with it. (That was the very tomb on which Father Païssy had found Alyosha sitting that morning.) Another memory cherished in the monastery was that of the famous Father Varsonofy, who had died only recently and had preceded Father Zossima as elder. During his lifetime all the pilgrims to the monastery had revered him as a crazy saint. There was a tradition that both of these men had lain in their coffins as though alive, that they had shown no signs of decomposition when they were buried, and that a holy light had shone in their faces. Some people even insisted that a sweet fragrance had come from their bodies.

Yet in spite of these edifying memories, it would be hard to explain the frivolity, absurdity and malice that showed themselves beside Father Zossima’s coffin. In my private opinion, several different causes were at work at the same time. One was a deep-rooted hostility to the institution of elders as a pernicious innovation, an antipathy hidden deep in the hearts of many of the monks. Even more powerful was jealousy of the dead man’s saintliness, which had been so firmly established during his lifetime that it was almost forbidden to question it. The late elder had won many hearts, more by love than by miracles, and had gathered around him a mass of loving followers. None the less, or rather all the more on that account, he had awakened jealousy and so had come to have bitter enemies, secret and open, not only in the monastery but in the world outside it. He did no one any harm, but “Why do they think him so saintly?” That question alone, repeated again and again, gave rise at last to an intense, insatiable hatred of him. That, I believe, was why many people were extremely delighted at the smell of decomposition that came so quickly, when not a day had passed since his death. At the same time, some of those who had until then been reverently devoted to the elder were almost mortified and personally affronted by this incident. This was how it happened.

Once the signs of decomposition had begun to appear, the monks’ faces gave away their secret reasons for going into the cell. They went in, stayed a little while, and hurried out to confirm the news to the other monks crowded outside. Some of these shook their heads sadly. Others did not even try to hide the delight that gleamed plainly in their malignant eyes. And no one reproached them for it now, or spoke up in protest. This was strange, since most of the monks had been devoted to the dead elder. But it seemed that God had, this time, let the minority have the upper hand for a while.

Visitors from outside, particularly those of the educated class, soon went into the cell too, with the same spying intent. Few of the peasantry went in, though there were crowds of them at the gates of the hermitage. After three o’clock the rush of worldly visitors increased greatly, no doubt because of the shocking news. People came who would not otherwise have come that day and had not meant to, and among them were some personages of high standing. But outward decorum was still kept up. Father Païssy, with a stern face, went on reading the Gospel aloud, firmly and distinctly. He seemed not to notice what was going on around him, though in fact he had observed something unusual long before. But at last the murmurs, at first subdued and then gradually louder and more confident, reached even him. “It shows God’s judgment is not as man’s,” Father Païssy suddenly heard. The first to say it was a layman, an elderly official from the town, known as a man of great piety. But he only said aloud what the monks had been whispering for some time. They had reached this damning conclusion long before, and the worst of it was that a kind of triumphant satisfaction in it showed more plainly every moment. Soon they began to lay aside even outward decorum, and almost seemed to feel they had a sort of right to do so.
“Why should _this_ have happened?” some of the monks said, at first with a show of regret. “He had a small frame, and his flesh was dried up on his bones. What was there to decay?”

“It must be a sign from heaven,” others rushed to add, and nobody objected; that view was taken up at once. People also pointed out that natural decay, as in any dead sinner, would have shown later, after twenty-four hours at least. This early rotting “was in excess of nature,” so the finger of God was plain. It was a sign. The argument seemed beyond answering.

Gentle Father Iosif, the librarian, one of the dead man’s great favorites, tried to answer some of the spiteful talkers. “This is not held everywhere alike,” he told them. Bodies of the just staying free of decay was no dogma of the Orthodox Church, he said, merely an opinion. Even in the most Orthodox lands, on Athos for instance, the smell of decay did not greatly disturb people. There the chief mark of a saved soul’s glorification was not an incorrupt body but the color of the bones, once the body had lain in the earth for many years and rotted away. “And if the bones are yellow as wax, that is the great sign that the Lord has glorified the dead saint. If they are black instead of yellow, it shows God did not think him worthy of such glory. That is what they believe on Athos, a great place, where Orthodox doctrine has been kept from ancient times, unbroken and in its purest form,” Father Iosif concluded.

But the meek Father’s words did little good and even brought a sneering answer. “That’s all pedantry and innovation, no point listening to it,” the monks decided. “We hold to the old teaching. Nowadays there are innovations of every kind. Do we have to follow them all?” others said.

“We’ve had as many holy fathers as they have. Look at them there among the Turks, they’ve forgotten everything. Their doctrine has been unclean for ages, and they haven’t even got bells,” the most sneering of them put in.

Father Iosif walked away, grieved all the more because he had put his opinion forward so timidly, as if he hardly believed it himself. He could see, to his distress, that something very unseemly was beginning, and that there were positive signs of disobedience. Little by little, all the sensible monks were reduced to silence, as Father Iosif had been. The result was that everyone who loved the elder and had accepted the eldership with devout obedience was all at once terribly cast down, and exchanged timid glances when they met. The enemies of elders, who saw the institution as a novelty, now carried their heads proudly. “The late elder Varsonofy gave off no smell of corruption, but a sweet fragrance,” they recalled with spite. “But he earned that glory not as an elder, but as a holy man.”

After that came a flood of criticism and even blame for Father Zossima. “His teaching was false. He taught that life is a great joy, not a vale of tears,” said some of the less reasonable. “He went along with the fashionable belief. He didn’t admit that hell has real fire,” others, still less reasonable, added. “He wasn’t strict about fasting. He treated himself to sweets, ate cherry jam with his tea. Ladies sent it to him. Is it right for a monk under strict rule to drink tea?” some of the envious were heard to say. “He sat in pride,” the most spiteful said vengefully. “He thought himself a saint, and took it as his due when people knelt to him.” “He abused the sacrament of confession,” the fiercest enemies of the eldership added in a malicious whisper. Some of the oldest monks were among them, the strictest in their devotion, true ascetics, who had held their tongues while the elder lived and now suddenly let them loose. This was terrible, because their words weighed heavily with the young monks, whose convictions were not yet firm. The monk from Obdorsk listened closely to all this, sighing deeply and nodding. “Yes, Father Ferapont was plainly right in what he said yesterday.” And at that very moment Father Ferapont himself arrived, as if on purpose to make the confusion worse.

I have already said that he rarely left his wooden cell by the apiary. He was hardly ever seen at church either. They excused this because he was crazy, and did not hold him to the rules that applied to everyone else. To tell the whole truth, though, they had little choice. It would have looked bad to press the common rules on such a great ascetic, who prayed day and night (he even dropped off to sleep on his knees). Had they insisted, the monks would have said, “He is holier than any of us, and his rule is harder than ours. If he stays away from church, it’s because he knows when he should go. He has a rule of his own.” To avoid sinful grumbling like this, Father Ferapont was left alone.

Everyone knew that Father Ferapont had a particular dislike of Father Zossima. Now word had reached him in his hut that “God’s judgment is not the same as man’s,” and that something had happened that was “in excess of nature.” We can fairly assume that one of the first to run to him with this news was the monk from Obdorsk, who had visited him the evening before and left his cell terror-stricken.

I have said above that Father Païssy stood firm and unmoving over the coffin, reading the Gospel, and could neither hear nor see what went on outside the cell. Still, he read most of it rightly in his heart, since he knew the men around him well. It did not shake him. He waited without fear for what would come next, watching shrewdly and keenly to see how the general excitement would end.

Suddenly a tremendous uproar in the passage, in open disregard of decorum, reached his ears. The door was thrown open, and Father Ferapont stood in the doorway. A crowd of monks could be seen behind him, with many townspeople. They did not enter the cell, though. They stayed at the foot of the steps, waiting to see what Father Ferapont would say or do. Bold as they were, they felt a certain awe and knew he had not come for nothing. Standing in the doorway, Father Ferapont raised his arms, and under his right arm the sharp, prying little eyes of the monk from Obdorsk peered in. He alone, so intensely curious, could not help running up the steps after Father Ferapont. The rest, by contrast, drew back in sudden alarm when the door crashed open. With his hands held high, Father Ferapont suddenly roared:

“Casting out I cast out!” And turning every which way, he began at once to make the sign of the cross toward each of the cell’s four walls and four corners, one after another. All who had come with Father Ferapont knew at once what he was doing. They knew he did this wherever he went, and that he would neither sit down nor say a word until he had driven out the evil spirits.
“Satan, get out! Satan, get out!” he said at each sign of the cross. “Casting out I cast out,” he roared again.

He wore his coarse gown belted with a rope. Under his hempen shirt his bare chest could be seen, covered with gray hair. His feet were bare. The moment he began waving his arms, the cruel irons he wore under his gown could be heard clanking.
Father Païssy broke off his reading, stepped forward and stood in front of him, waiting.
“Why have you come, worthy Father? Why do you break good order? Why do you trouble the peace of the flock?” he said at last, with a stern look.

“Why have I come? You ask me why? What is your faith?” Father Ferapont shouted, like a madman. “I’ve come to drive out your guests, the unclean devils. I’ve come to see how many have crowded in while I was away. I want to sweep them out with a birch broom.”
“You drive out the evil spirit, but maybe you serve him yourself,” Father Païssy went on, unafraid. “And who can say of himself, ‘I am holy’? Can you, Father?”

“I’m unclean, not holy. I wouldn’t sit in an armchair, and I wouldn’t let them bow down to me like an idol,” Father Ferapont thundered. “These days folk are destroying the true faith. The dead man, your saint,” and he turned to the crowd and pointed at the coffin, “didn’t believe in devils. He gave out medicine against the devils. So now they’re as thick as spiders in the corners. And now he himself has started to stink. In that we see a great sign from God.”

What he meant was this. One of the monks was tormented by visions of evil spirits, in his dreams and later even awake. In deadly terror he told Father Zossima, and the elder told him to pray without ceasing and fast strictly. When that did no good, the elder told him to take a certain medicine as well, while going on with prayer and fasting. Many were shocked at the time and shook their heads over it, and Father Ferapont most of all, since some of the fault-finders had rushed to report to him this “extraordinary” advice from the elder.

“Go away, Father!” Father Païssy said, in a voice of command. “Judging is for God, not for man. Perhaps what we see here is a ‘sign’ that you cannot understand, nor I, nor any of us. Go, Father, and do not disturb the flock!” he repeated with emphasis.

“He didn’t keep the fasts by the rule, and that’s why the sign has come. That’s plain, and it’s a sin to hide it,” the fanatic answered, swept along by a zeal that ran ahead of his reason, and he would not be quiet. “Sweetmeats led him astray. Ladies brought them to him in their pockets. He sipped tea, he worshiped his belly, stuffing it with sweet things and his mind with proud thoughts.... And for this he’s put to shame....”

“You are speaking rashly, Father.” Father Païssy, too, raised his voice. “I admire your fasting and your hardships, but you talk rashly, like some frivolous boy, fickle and childish. Go away, Father. I command you!” Father Païssy thundered, finishing.

“I’m going,” said Ferapont, looking a little thrown, but just as bitter. “You learned men! You’re so clever you look down on my lowliness. I came here with little learning, and what I did know I’ve forgotten here. God Himself has protected me in my weakness from your cleverness.”

Father Païssy stood over him, resolute, waiting. Father Ferapont fell silent. Then, suddenly resting his cheek on his hand in dejection, he said in a sing-song voice, with his eyes on the dead elder’s coffin:

“Tomorrow they’ll sing ‘Our Helper and Defender’ over him—a splendid anthem—and over me, when I die, they’ll sing only ‘What earthly joy’—a little canticle,”[6] he added with tearful regret. “You’re proud and puffed up. This place is vanity!” he suddenly shouted like a madman, and with a wave of his hand he turned sharply and hurried down the steps. The crowd waiting below wavered. Some followed him at once, some hung back, since the cell was still open, and Father Païssy came out onto the steps after Father Ferapont and stood watching him. But the worked-up old fanatic was not entirely silenced. Twenty steps off, he suddenly turned toward the setting sun, threw up both arms and, as if someone had cut him down, dropped to the ground with a loud scream.

“My God has conquered! Christ has conquered the setting sun!” he shouted wildly, stretching his hands up toward the sun. Then he fell on his face and sobbed like a small child, his body shaking with tears, his arms spread out on the ground. At that they all rushed up to him. There were cries and sobs of sympathy ... a sort of frenzy seemed to seize them all.
“This is the one who is a saint! This is the one who is a holy man!” some cried out, their fear gone. “This is the one who ought to be elder,” others added spitefully.

“He wouldn’t be elder ... he’d refuse ... he wouldn’t serve a cursed innovation ... he wouldn’t copy their foolery,” other voices joined in at once. It is hard to say how far they might have gone, but just then the bell rang for service. They all began to cross themselves together. Father Ferapont, too, got up and, crossing himself, went back to his cell without looking round, still crying out words that made no sense at all. A few went after him, but most scattered, hurrying to service. Father Païssy had Father Iosif read in his place and went down. The wild shouting of bigots could not shake him, but his heart was suddenly filled with sadness, for some particular reason, and he felt it. He stopped and asked himself suddenly, “Why am I sad, even to dejection?” and at once realized, to his surprise, that his sudden sadness had a very small and particular cause. In the crowd packed at the entrance to the cell, he had noticed Alyosha, and he remembered that at the sight of him he had felt a pang in his heart. “Can that boy mean so much to my heart now?” he asked himself, wondering.

Just then Alyosha went past him, hurrying off, though not toward the church. Their eyes met. Alyosha looked away quickly and lowered his eyes to the ground, and from the boy’s look alone Father Païssy guessed what a great change was taking place in him at that moment.
“Have you, too, fallen into temptation?” cried Father Païssy. “Can you be with those of little faith?” he added sadly.

Alyosha stopped and looked blankly at Father Païssy, then quickly looked away again and again stared at the ground. He stood turned aside and kept his face from Father Païssy, who watched him closely.
“Where are you rushing off to? The bell is calling to service,” he asked again, but again Alyosha gave no answer.
“Are you leaving the hermitage? What, without asking leave, without asking a blessing?”

Alyosha suddenly smiled a twisted smile and gave a strange, very strange, look to the Father into whose care his former guide, the former master of his heart and mind, his beloved elder, had entrusted him as he lay dying. Then, still without a word, he waved his hand, as if he did not even care to be respectful, and walked off with quick steps toward the gates, away from the hermitage.
“You’ll come back again!” Father Païssy murmured, looking after him in sorrow and surprise.
